templates.title: Sync, microtask, macrotask
templates.prompt: Read the code and predict exactly what it prints, in order. Everything here is synchronous, a microtask, or a macrotask — the order they run in is the whole question.
templates.objective: Separate synchronous execution from the microtask queue and the macrotask queue.
hints: Synchronous statements finish before any callback runs.
Promise callbacks and setTimeout callbacks are not in the same queue.
templates.explanation: All synchronous code runs to completion first. Then the microtask queue drains fully — that is where promise callbacks live. Only then does the event loop take one macrotask, which is where setTimeout lands. A zero millisecond timeout is not immediate; it is merely eligible.
weakAnswerSignals: Assumes setTimeout with zero delay runs immediately
Interleaves the callbacks with synchronous logs
followUpPrompts: Where would queueMicrotask land in this order?
mayaPushbacks: Why does a zero millisecond delay not mean immediately?

templates.title: A microtask queued from a microtask
templates.prompt: Both chains are already resolved, so both callbacks are queued immediately. One of them queues a third. Predict what prints, in order.
templates.objective: Show that a microtask queued during the drain runs after the ones already waiting.
hints: Both outer callbacks are queued before the first one runs.
A microtask created during the drain goes to the back of the queue.
templates.explanation: Both outer callbacks are queued before either runs, so the queue holds a then c. Running a appends b to the back of the same queue, not the front. The loop keeps draining, so c runs before b. New microtasks join the end of the line.
weakAnswerSignals: Assumes a nested promise runs immediately
Predicts a, b, c
followUpPrompts: What if the inner promise were a setTimeout instead?
mayaPushbacks: Why does the nested callback not jump ahead of one already queued?

templates.title: await is a pause, not a wait
templates.prompt: This async function awaits a value that is not a promise. Predict what prints, in order.
templates.objective: Show that await always yields, even when there is nothing to wait for.
hints: Code before the first await runs synchronously.
await suspends even when the awaited value is already available.
templates.explanation: An async function runs synchronously until its first await. So 1 prints immediately. await null still suspends the function and queues the rest as a microtask, letting 3 print. Only when the stack is empty does 2 run. Awaiting a non-promise still costs you a turn.
goodAnswerSignals: Knows the body runs synchronously up to the first await
weakAnswerSignals: Assumes the whole async body is deferred
Assumes await null does not suspend
followUpPrompts: What changes if you remove the await entirely?
mayaPushbacks: Why does awaiting a non-promise still defer the rest?

templates.title: var, closures, and the loop that already finished
templates.prompt: A classic. Predict what this prints, in order, and be precise about how many lines there are.
templates.objective: Show that var is function-scoped, so every callback closes over one shared binding.
hints: var is scoped to the function, not the loop body.
The callbacks run after the loop has completely finished.
templates.explanation: var creates a single binding for the whole function, not one per iteration. All three callbacks close over that same variable. By the time the timeouts run, the loop has finished and i is 3. Replacing var with let creates a fresh binding per iteration and prints 0, 1, 2.
goodAnswerSignals: Knows let would change the answer
weakAnswerSignals: Predicts 0, 1, 2
Thinks each iteration captures its own copy
followUpPrompts: What exactly does let change about the binding?
mayaPushbacks: How many bindings of i exist in this program?

templates.title: Two loops, two capture rules
templates.prompt: Both loops push functions into the same array. Only the declaration keyword differs. Predict the single line this prints.
templates.objective: Contrast per-iteration bindings with a single shared binding in one output.
hints: The two loops differ only in the declaration keyword.
One keyword creates three bindings, the other creates one.
templates.explanation: let gives each iteration its own binding, so those three closures capture 0, 1 and 2. var gives one binding for all three, and after the loop it holds 3. The same loop shape produces completely different closures depending on the keyword.
goodAnswerSignals: Gets both halves of the line right
weakAnswerSignals: Predicts all zeros or all threes
Applies one rule to both loops
followUpPrompts: Rewrite the var loop so it behaves like the let loop.
mayaPushbacks: Why does let create a new binding each iteration?

templates.title: Hoisted, but not initialised
templates.prompt: One of these reads happens before the declaration and survives. The other throws. Predict what prints, in order.
templates.objective: Distinguish var hoisting from the temporal dead zone that let and const create.
hints: Both declarations are hoisted; only one is initialised early.
The error type is the specific detail being tested.
templates.explanation: var declarations are hoisted and initialised to undefined, so reading a early is legal and gives undefined. let is also hoisted but stays uninitialised until its declaration runs — the temporal dead zone — and reading it there throws a ReferenceError, not undefined and not a TypeError.
weakAnswerSignals: Predicts undefined for both
Guesses TypeError
followUpPrompts: What would typeof b print inside the try block?
mayaPushbacks: If let is hoisted too, why does reading it throw?

templates.title: Copies that are not copies
templates.prompt: One assignment shares a reference, the other creates a shallow copy. Predict what prints, in order.
templates.objective: Separate copying a reference from copying the object it points at.
hints: Only one of these two statements creates a new object.
const does not make the object immutable.
templates.explanation: const b = a copies the reference, so a and b are the same object and mutating one shows in the other. Spreading into c builds a new object, so writing to c leaves a untouched. const protects the binding, never the contents.
goodAnswerSignals: Distinguishes the binding from the object
weakAnswerSignals: Assumes const prevents mutation
Predicts 1 for the first log

templates.title: map takes a snapshot
templates.prompt: The array is mutated after map has already run. Predict what prints, in order.
templates.objective: Show that map produces a new array that does not track later mutations.
hints: map returns a new array rather than a view.
The push happens after map has finished.
templates.explanation: map walks the array once and returns a new array built from what it found. Pushing to the original afterwards has no effect on the result — there is no live link between them. This is why mapped state in a UI goes stale unless it is recomputed.
goodAnswerSignals: Knows map is eager and returns a new array
weakAnswerSignals: Thinks the mapped array tracks the source
Predicts 4 and 4
followUpPrompts: What if you mutated an object inside the array instead of pushing?
mayaPushbacks: Is there any link between the two arrays after map returns?

templates.title: A rejection is still a microtask
templates.prompt: The async function throws immediately, but the catch handler is not synchronous. Predict what prints, in order.
templates.objective: Show that a rejection handler runs as a microtask, not at the moment of the throw.
hints: A throw inside an async function becomes a rejected promise.
The catch callback is scheduled, not run immediately.
templates.explanation: Throwing inside an async function rejects its promise rather than propagating up the stack. The catch callback is scheduled as a microtask, so the synchronous log runs first. This is why wrapping an async call in a plain try/catch without await catches nothing.
goodAnswerSignals: Places caught after the sync log
weakAnswerSignals: Expects caught to print first
Thinks a plain try/catch would work here
followUpPrompts: Would a synchronous try/catch around boom() catch this?
mayaPushbacks: Why does the throw not interrupt the synchronous log?

templates.title: Concurrent awaits interleave
templates.prompt: Two async calls are started before either is awaited. Predict the single line printed at the end.
templates.objective: Show that starting two async functions interleaves them at each await point.
hints: Both calls run before Promise.all awaits anything.
Each function runs synchronously up to its first await.
templates.explanation: Calling task(1) runs synchronously to its await and suspends, then task(2) does the same — so both starts happen before either end. Each suspension queues the remainder as a microtask, and they resume in the order they suspended. Concurrency here is interleaving on one thread, not parallelism.
goodAnswerSignals: Groups the starts before the ends
weakAnswerSignals: Predicts start1,end1,start2,end2
Confuses concurrency with parallelism
followUpPrompts: How would the output change with await task(1); await task(2);?
mayaPushbacks: Are these two functions running in parallel?
